Conversion Equations Between Measurement Methods

Source: R/method_convert.R
method_convert.Rd

Estimates the linear relation between each pair of methods, as conversion equations from one method to another with prediction limits. The bias between methods may be constant (from a method_vc() fit), change linearly with the level of measurement (regression of the differences on the averages; Carstensen, 2010, section 4.7), or follow the scaled model, in which each method is a linear function of a common true value (Carstensen, 2010, ch. 7).

Usage

method_convert(
  data = NULL,
  y,
  method,
  id,
  replicate = NULL,
  bias = c("linear", "scaled"),
  variance = c("constant", "linear"),
  replicates = c("exchangeable", "linked"),
  pred_level = 0.95,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  transform = "none",
  ci_method = c("delta", "boot"),
  estimator = c("altreg", "ml"),
  boot_reps = 999,
  pair_seed = NULL,
  max_iter = 100,
  tol = 1e-06,
  object = NULL,
  keep_model = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame in long format (one row per measurement). Not needed when object is supplied.

y

Name of the column with the measurements.

method

Name of the column identifying the method. The first level (if a factor) or the first value in sorted order is the reference method; differences are reported as earlier minus later level.

id

Name of the column identifying the item (subject).

replicate

Name of the column identifying the replicate. Required when an item is measured more than once by the same method.

bias

Model for the bias between methods. "linear" (default): regression of the differences on the averages for each pair of methods. "scaled": the scaled model, fit by alternating regression or maximum likelihood (see estimator; requires replicates). See details.

variance

Model for the SD of the differences with bias = "linear": "constant" (default) or "linear" in the average.

replicates

Whether replicates are "exchangeable" (default) or "linked"; see method_vc(). Exchangeable replicates are paired at random within item (see pair_seed), linked replicates by replicate.

pred_level

Coverage of the prediction limits. Default is 0.95.

conf_level

Confidence level for the conversion parameters. Default is 0.95.

transform

Transformation applied to the measurements before analysis: "none" (default), "log", "logit", "pctlogit" (logit of a percentage), "sqrt", "asinsqrt", or a list with functions fun and inv (its inverse) and, optionally, a name. All estimates are on the transformed scale.

ci_method

Method for the confidence intervals of the conversion parameters: "delta" (default; delta method) or, for bias = "scaled" with estimator = "altreg", "boot" (parametric bootstrap). See details.

estimator

For bias = "scaled", how the model is fit: "altreg" (default; alternating regression, as in MethComp) or "ml" (maximum likelihood of the structural model with the lavaan package, which must be installed). Use "ml" for confidence intervals with close to the stated coverage. See details.

boot_reps

Number of bootstrap replicates for ci_method = "boot". Default is 999. Each replicate refits the model, so this can take several minutes; set a seed with set.seed() for reproducible intervals.

pair_seed

Seed for the random pairing of exchangeable replicates; the global random number generator state is restored afterwards.

max_iter, tol

Iteration limit and convergence tolerance (largest relative change in the conversion parameters and SDs) for bias = "scaled". Bootstrap refits use a tolerance of at least 1e-4.

object

A method_vc() fit (simple_mvc). If supplied, the data and column arguments are ignored and the conversions are derived from its estimates with a constant bias (slope 1).

keep_model

Logical. Whether to keep the fitted models. Default is TRUE.

Value

An object of class simple_mconv, a list with:

  • conversion: tibble with one row per ordered pair (to, from), including each method to itself: the intercept alpha, slope beta, prediction SD sd_pred, their standard errors and df, and confidence limits (alpha_lower, alpha_upper, beta_lower, beta_upper; and, for the scaled model, sd_lower, sd_upper with the bootstrap or estimator = "ml").

  • limits_par: list, by ordered pair (named "to|from"), of the parameters used to evaluate the prediction limits at any level.

  • da: for bias = "linear", tibble of the DA regressions for each pair (a, b and their SEs, s, c_sd, d_sd, df, numbers of pairs and items, and whether the SEs are cluster-robust).

  • varcomp: the variance components (for the scaled model, on each method's scale, with bootstrap intervals if requested; for a conversion from a method_vc() fit, its variance components); otherwise NULL.

  • vc_fit: for a conversion from a method_vc() fit, its bias and limits tables at pred_level and conf_level, and its design (used by the Bland-Altman plot); otherwise absent.

  • scaled: for the scaled model, the per-method intercepts and slopes, the item values, the variance components on the scale of the true values, and the iteration history of the alternating regression (trace; NULL with estimator = "ml"). With estimator = "ml", the item values are the factor scores of the true values.

  • boot: for ci_method = "boot", the matrix of bootstrap estimates.

  • data: the processed data.

  • pairs: list of the paired data used for each pair of methods.

  • transform: the transformation (functions included).

  • model: list of the fitted lm objects (linear bias), the final variance component model (scaled, alternating regression), the lavaan fit (scaled, estimator = "ml"), or NULL.

  • fit_info: list describing the fit and settings (including the estimator, number of iterations, convergence, and failed bootstrap refits; with estimator = "ml", also the log-likelihood logl, the names of zero or negative variance estimates heywood, and fit_measures: chi-square, df, p value, RMSEA and SRMR).

  • call: the matched call, with evaluated settings.

Details

Constant bias (object supplied): the conversion from method m to method k is \(y_k = (\alpha_k - \alpha_m) + y_m\), with prediction SD \(\sqrt{V_{mk}}\) from method_vc() (Carstensen, 2010, ch. 5), and \(\sqrt{2}\sigma_m\) for two measurements by the same method (with replicates).

Linear bias (bias = "linear"): for each pair, with differences \(D = y_1 - y_2\) and averages \(A = (y_1 + y_2)/2\) on the (transformed) scale, \(D = a + bA + e\) is fit by least squares. With variance = "constant", \(SD(e) = s\); with variance = "linear", \(SD(e \mid A) = c' + d'A\), from regressing the absolute residuals on \(A\) (multiplied by \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\)). The relation is converted to $$y_1 = \frac{a}{1 - b/2} + \frac{1 + b/2}{1 - b/2} y_2,$$ and the prediction limits are the lines \(D = (a \pm z c') + (b \pm z d')A\) (with \(c' = s, d' = 0\) for constant variance) transformed the same way (Carstensen, 2010, eq. 4.11); the conversion from \(y_1\) to \(y_2\) inverts these lines. This requires \(|b| < 2\). With constant variance the prediction SD is \(s/(1 - b/2)\) (to method 1) and \(s/(1 + b/2)\) (to method 2); with linear variance it depends on the level and is reported as NA.

When items contribute several pairs (replicates), the covariance of \((a, b)\) is cluster-robust by item, with (items - 1) degrees of freedom. Confidence intervals for the conversion intercepts and slopes use the delta method.

A slope of the differences on the averages does not by itself show that the methods are related by a slope other than 1. Whenever the two methods have unequal measurement error variances, cov(D, A) = (var(y1) - var(y2)) / 2 is not zero, so \(b\) is biased away from zero (Bland & Altman, 1999). The scaled model (bias = "scaled") or errors-in-variables regression (dem_reg(), pb_reg()) account for the measurement errors.

Scaled model (bias = "scaled"): measurement r of item i by method m is $$y_{mir} = \alpha_m + \beta_m(\mu_i + a_{ir} + c_{mi}) + e_{mir},$$ with the variance components of method_vc() on the scale of the true values \(\mu_i\) (Carstensen, 2010, eq. 7.1). With estimator = "altreg" (default) it is fit by alternating regression as in the AltReg() function of the MethComp package: each method is regressed on the current predicted true values \(\mu_i + a_{ir} + c_{mi}\) (with a random item intercept), and the variance component model is refit to \((y - \alpha_m)/\beta_m\), until the conversions converge. The conversion from method m to k is \(\alpha_{k|m} = \alpha_k - \alpha_m\beta_k/\beta_m\), \(\beta_{k|m} = \beta_k/\beta_m\), with prediction SD \(\sqrt{\tau_k^2 + \sigma_k^2 + \beta_{k|m}^2(\tau_m^2 + \sigma_m^2)}\) from the variance components on each method's scale (\(\omega\) cancels), and \(\sqrt{2}\sigma_m\) for a method to itself. As in MethComp, the method-by-item SD is multiplied by \(I/(I-2)\). The per-method \(\alpha_m, \beta_m\) are reported with the first method as reference (\(\alpha = 0, \beta = 1\)); the conversions do not depend on this choice.

With estimator = "ml", the true values are also treated as random, \(\mu_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma_\mu^2)\) (the structural model), and the model is fit by full maximum likelihood with the lavaan package, as a confirmatory factor model with equality constraints (one row per item; missing measurements by full-information ML, so the design need not be balanced). The alternating regression supplies the starting values. The method-by-item variance is common to all methods on the scale of the true values, as above, but is not multiplied by \(I/(I-2)\), so with few items the prediction SDs are a little smaller (on average by 3% to 5% with 15 items and about 1% with 60 items, in the simulations below). The two fits estimate the same model, but they weight the data differently, and their estimates can differ when the true values are far from normal; for the oximetry data in MethComp (skewed true values), the slope of pulse on CO is 0.94 by alternating regression and 0.90 by maximum likelihood (95% CI 0.80 to 1.00). The summary reports the model's chi-square test of fit, RMSEA and SRMR. Variance estimates can be zero or negative (Heywood cases), mostly with fewer than about 20 items; this gives a warning, and the corresponding SDs are reported as 0.

Confidence intervals for the scaled model with estimator = "ml" are Wald intervals from the ML standard errors (delta method for the conversions), with t quantiles on \(I - 1\) degrees of freedom (\(I\) items); the prediction SD intervals are computed on the log scale. In simulations (15, 30 or 60 items; 2 or 3 methods; 3 replicates, linked or exchangeable; balanced data, 15% of the measurements missing, or uniform or skewed true values; 500 data sets each), 95% intervals for the conversion intercepts and slopes covered the true values 92% to 97% of the time (on average 93.6% with 15 items, 94.5% with 30 and 95.1% with 60), and those for the prediction SDs 92% to 95%. Wald intervals with normal quantiles, or with robust (sandwich) standard errors, covered less. No intervals are given for the variance components.

With estimator = "altreg", "delta" (default) uses the standard errors of \((\alpha_m, \beta_m)\) from the final regressions of each method on the predicted true values. These treat the predicted true values as known, so they are much too narrow: in the same simulations (balanced data, normal true values), 95% intervals for the conversion intercepts and slopes covered the true values only 53% to 73% of the time, with no improvement with more items. They are useful only as a rough indication of precision. "boot" simulates data from the fitted model with the observed design (the same items, methods, and replicates, and the fitted item values), refits the model, and reports percentile intervals for the conversion parameters, the prediction SDs, and the variance components. The bootstrap may improve on the delta method, but its coverage has not been checked by simulation, and each replicate refits the model (999 replicates can take several minutes). MethComp itself gives no intervals for the alternating regression. The conversions and prediction limits themselves do not depend on ci_method.

All estimates are on the transformed scale; predict() and the conversion plot back-transform the conversions and limits to the original scale (Carstensen, 2010, ch. 8).

References

Carstensen, B. (2010). Comparing Clinical Measurement Methods: A Practical Guide. Wiley.

Bland, J. M., & Altman, D. G. (1999). Measuring agreement in method comparison studies. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 8(2), 135-160.

See also

simple_mconv-methods, method_vc(), dem_reg(), pb_reg()

Examples

dat = sim_methods(n_items = 50, n_reps = 2, methods = c("A", "B"),
                  alpha = c(0, 1), beta = c(1, 1.2), mu_mean = 10,
                  mu_sd = 3, tau = 0.2, sigma = 0.3, seed = 1)

# linear bias
conv = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                      replicate = "repl", pair_seed = 1)
conv
#> Conversion Between Methods: Linear Bias
#> y(To) = alpha + beta * y(From); sd = prediction SD
#> Regression of differences on averages, constant SD of the differences
#> 
#>  To From alpha   95% CI             beta   95% CI           sd    
#>  A  A     0.0000                    1.0000                        
#>  A  B    -0.8536 [-1.3802, -0.3269] 0.8345 [0.7978, 0.8712] 0.4429
#>  B  A     1.0228 [ 0.4360,  1.6097] 1.1983 [1.1456, 1.2511] 0.5308
#>  B  B     0.0000                    1.0000                        
#> 
#> CIs: approximate (delta method, cluster-robust by item)
#> A slope of the differences on the averages can arise from unequal measurement errors alone;
#>   see ?method_convert
predict(conv, newdata = c(5, 10, 15), from = "A", to = "B")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   from_value   fit lower upper
#>        <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1          5  7.01  5.97  8.05
#> 2         10 13.0  12.0  14.0 
#> 3         15 19.0  18.0  20.0 

# constant bias, from a variance component fit
fit = method_vc(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                replicate = "repl")
method_convert(object = fit)
#> Conversion Between Methods: Constant Bias
#> y(To) = alpha + beta * y(From); sd = prediction SD
#> 
#>  To From alpha  95% CI             beta 95% CI sd    
#>  A  A     0.000                    1           0.4434
#>  A  B    -3.068 [-3.2464, -2.8895] 1           0.7005
#>  B  A     3.068 [ 2.8895,  3.2464] 1           0.7005
#>  B  B     0.000                    1           0.4343
#> 
#> From method_vc(): slope fixed at 1; intercept CIs are those of the biases

# scaled model (alternating regression)
sc = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                    replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled", tol = 1e-4)
sc
#> Conversion Between Methods: Scaled Model
#> y(To) = alpha + beta * y(From); sd = prediction SD
#> 
#>  To From alpha   95% CI             beta   95% CI           sd    
#>  A  A     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4434
#>  A  B    -0.8468 [-1.1599, -0.5336] 0.8340 [0.8111, 0.8568] 0.4573
#>  B  A     1.0153 [ 0.6670,  1.3637] 1.1991 [1.1662, 1.2319] 0.5484
#>  B  B     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4343
#> 
#> CIs: delta method, conditional on the predicted true values;
#>   much too narrow (about 55-75% coverage for 95% in simulations);
#>   use estimator = 'ml' for intervals; see ?method_convert
#> Alternating regression: 3 iterations, converged (criterion 5.87e-05)
#> 
#> Variance components (SD, on each method's scale)
#>  Method tau    sigma 
#>  A      0.1504 0.3136
#>  B      0.1803 0.3071

# scaled model by maximum likelihood (needs lavaan), with intervals that
# have close to the stated coverage
if (requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)) {
  method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                 replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled", estimator = "ml",
                 tol = 1e-4)
}
#> Conversion Between Methods: Scaled Model (maximum likelihood)
#> y(To) = alpha + beta * y(From); sd = prediction SD
#> 
#>  To From alpha   95% CI             beta   95% CI           sd    
#>  A  A     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4434
#>  A  B    -0.8394 [-1.3054, -0.3733] 0.8334 [0.7994, 0.8675] 0.4533
#>  B  A     1.0071 [ 0.4880,  1.5262] 1.1998 [1.1509, 1.2488] 0.5439
#>  B  B     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4343
#> 
#> CIs: Wald (maximum likelihood, structural model), t with items - 1 df;
#>   about 92-97% coverage for 95% in simulations with 15-60 items; see ?method_convert
#> Maximum likelihood (lavaan): 22 iterations, converged; log-likelihood -203.15
#> 
#> Variance components (SD, on each method's scale)
#>  Method tau    sigma 
#>  A      0.1443 0.3136
#>  B      0.1732 0.3071
# \donttest{
# parametric bootstrap intervals (use more replicates in practice)
set.seed(1)
method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
               replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled", tol = 1e-4,
               ci_method = "boot", boot_reps = 50)
#> Conversion Between Methods: Scaled Model
#> y(To) = alpha + beta * y(From); sd = prediction SD
#> 
#>  To From alpha   95% CI             beta   95% CI           sd    
#>  A  A     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4434
#>  A  B    -0.8468 [-1.2489, -0.3245] 0.8340 [0.7921, 0.8622] 0.4573
#>  B  A     1.0153 [ 0.4097,  1.4494] 1.1991 [1.1598, 1.2624] 0.5484
#>  B  B     0.0000                    1.0000                  0.4343
#> 
#> CIs: parametric bootstrap percentile intervals (50 of 50 refits used); approximate, coverage not yet evaluated
#> Alternating regression: 3 iterations, converged (criterion 5.87e-05)
#> 
#> Variance components (SD, on each method's scale)
#>  Method tau    sigma 
#>  A      0.1504 0.3136
#>  B      0.1803 0.3071
# }
